title: Why School Teaches You Things You'll Never Use
tags: useless things we learn in school
description:
Why do we spend years learning equations, formulas and concepts that most of us may never directly use again?

It is one of the most common complaints about education. You learn algebra, trigonometry, physics and complicated equations in school, only to grow up and realise that everyday life rarely asks you to solve any of them.

But perhaps we are asking the wrong question.

In this video, we look at why seemingly “useless” exercises can still have a purpose. A cricketer does push-ups without ever doing them during a match. A learner driver practises manoeuvres they may never repeat after the test. A programmer starts with “Hello World” even though no one builds a career doing that. Mathematics can work in much the same way.

The equation may not be the final goal. What you are training yourself to do while solving it may be far more important.

But there is an equally important catch. This argument cannot be used to justify rote learning, memorising formulas without understanding them, or assuming that everything inside a textbook is automatically valuable.

So perhaps the real question is not, “When will I ever use this?”

Perhaps it is:

After spending all those years in school, did education actually train us to think?

Let me know what you think in the comments. What is something you studied in school that you thought was completely useless? Looking back today, do you still think it was useless?


Why study math when you will never use it? Discover the reality behind physics equations and whether your math textbook study matters.

Many students dread the late nights spent solving equations that seem disconnected from daily life. This video addresses the frustration of academic requirements and offers a perspective on why we are pushed to learn these complex subjects. It is designed for anyone feeling burnt out by schoolwork and questioning the practical value of their current curriculum.

By examining the purpose of these lessons, you will learn to reframe how you approach physics equations and understand the broader goal of formal education. We break down the necessity of learning mathematics even when the immediate application feels absent. You will walk away with a clearer understanding of why your math textbook study is structured this way.

transcript: If Newton had never invented it, I wouldn't have had to study it. You probably heard that joke. You may have said something very similar yourself, especially on one of those nights when an examination is approaching and you're sitting in front of a mathematics or a physics textbook wondering why on earth you're solving an equation that seems to have nothing to do with the life you're going to live. And it is a perfectly reasonable question. Think about it. Most of us learn algebra, geometry, trigonometry, and physics in school. But after leaving school, how many of us actually sit down one morning and say, "Okay, today I think I will solve a quadratic equation before breakfast." We don't. We use mathematics all the time, that's for sure, but the kind we use in everyday life is fairly simple. We calculate how much something costs, work out a percentage, compare two prices, manage our money. We don't usually stand in a supermarket wondering whether the quadratic formula can help us choose the brand of biscuits that we need. So then, why did we study it? This is one of the biggest complaints people have about education. We spend a large part of our childhood and youth learning things and later discover we don't directly use most of them. So perhaps the education system really is wasting our time. Or perhaps we are asking the wrong question. Because when we ask, "When am I ever going to use this?" we are assuming that the only reason to learn something is that we will eventually use that exact piece of knowledge somewhere in our life. And that is not really how learning works. Imagine a professional cricketer. Before that person gets on the field to play, they spend a lot of time doing things that have nothing to do hitting a ball, running, strength exercises, the same drills again and again. Nobody watches a cricketer doing push-ups and says, "What is the point? He isn't going to do push-ups in the middle of a match." But we understand why the push-up is there. It isn't the thing the cricketer is trying to get good at. It is the part of the training that helps him get good at something else. Driving lessons work the same way. You practice reversing through a particular path or drive through a H-shaped or figure-eight course because you need to demonstrate those skills to pass the driving test. But once you get your license, you will probably never encounter those exercises again. The exercise was never the point. It was training your ability to control the car and respond to different situations. And that gives us a possible answer about mathematics. Maybe you didn't learn the quadratic equation because you were going to use a quadratic equation at 40. The quadratic equation is the push-up. What matters is what happens while you're trying to solve it. You have to understand what the problem is asking, decide what information is important, work through it step by step. Notice when something has gone wrong, you have to go back to find the mistake. Look at the answer and ask whether it actually makes sense. Do that once and not much changes. But do it for years across different kinds of problems and something slowly happens. You get comfortable taking something confusing and breaking it into parts you can actually deal with. That ability is useful even when the problem has nothing to do with mathematics. That is also why beginners learning to program are given absurdly simple task, a program that adds two numbers or one that prints "Hello world." No professional programmer gets paid to add two numbers. That was never why the exercise existed. The beginner needs a simple problem to understand how the computer works, how instructions are written, how one thing leads to another before they can move on to something harder. The first program isn't important because of what it does. It is important because of what the learner is practicing. Mathematics and physics and all the sciences works exactly the same way. There is something else that happens when you learn a subject properly. You start seeing the world differently because of it. A person who has never studied astronomy can look up at a night sky and see a beautiful scatter of stars, but someone who has studied astronomy looks at exactly the same sky and starts thinking about distances, stellar evolution, galaxies, and the enormous stretches of space sitting between those points of light. The sky hasn't changed. Neither person is looking at the wrong thing. One of them simply has more ways of understanding what they are looking at. And that is one of the nicest things education can do. Give you another way of looking at something that was already there. But the universe is far bigger than the part of it we experience directly. Go down to the scale of atoms and [music] things stop behaving the way our everyday intuition expects. Get close to the speed of light and our ordinary ideas about space and time stop being enough. Our senses have limits, too. We can't see most of the electromagnetic spectrum. We can't hear most sound We can't look at an atom and see what it's doing. So, if we want to understand what our senses cannot directly show us, we need other tools. That is where mathematics comes in. A way to talk about things we cannot see or touch. To describe relationships and patterns that aren't obvious from observation. Physics runs on abstraction the same way. Just often at a far more demanding level. That is also why you can't jump straight from school level physics to something like general relativity. Nobody decided to make physics unnecessarily hard. You need one idea before the next one makes sense. One tool before the next tool becomes useful. It is a lot like learning music. When someone starts learning the piano, practicing scales isn't particularly exciting. Nobody grows up dreaming of playing scales on a stage. But the point of scales was never to become good at scales. It is to make it possible years later to sit down and actually play something that moves people. Skip the scales and you don't get to skip straight to the music. You just never get there. Mathematics works the same way in physics. The equation in front of you right now isn't standing between you and the interesting part of the subject. It is how you get there. You just can't see that yet while you're still learning the basics. So, what does useful even mean here? If useful means something I will directly use in my job, a lot of education looks useless. But if useful means something that helps me understand the world, solve problems, and think [music] more clearly, the answer changes completely. There is an important catch, though. This isn't an excuse to defend everything that happens in a classroom. Something being in a textbook doesn't automatically make it valuable. Mathematics can build problem-solving skills, but that doesn't mean making students memorize formulas is good teaching. Science being in the curriculum doesn't mean a student has actually learned to think scientifically. A student can memorize Newton's laws and still have no idea what they mean. Reproduce a formula perfectly in an exam and forget it months later. So, there are really two separate questions. One, does the subject itself have a reason to be taught? Two, are we teaching it in a way that actually achieves that reason? And the distinctions matters a great deal once we start talking about education in India. The more interesting question is, after spending so many years in school, what have we actually trained the student [music] to do? Can they solve a problem they've never seen before? Understand an idea instead of just remembering its definition. Tell the difference between evidence and someone else's confident opinion. Say, "I don't know." when they don't know something. Change their mind when the evidence changes. And perhaps most importantly, can they look at something they have been told all their life and ask a simple question, "How do we know this is true?" If education teaches you to accept an answer without ever asking how we know it is correct, that is a very wrong way of learning. The equation you never use may just >> [music] >> have been a training exercise. The real question is whether the education system trained you to think. So, are complex equations the problem with our education system? Honestly, no. They're doing exactly what they're supposed to do. Building the muscle you will need for everything else, and giving you access to ideas your senses were never equipped to reach on their own.
